The fighting among the victorious mujahideen after the fall of Kabul in April 1992, which wrecked much of the capital and prepared the way for the Taliban.

An interim government was agreed in Peshawar, with Burhanuddin Rabbani becoming president, and Ahmad Shah Massoud as defence minister. Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, whose fighters had been left outside, refused to join. From 1992 his men fired rockets and artillery into Kabul almost daily, hitting homes, markets and hospitals. He was backed by Pakistan's ISI. In 1994 Dostum switched sides and joined him, and the city's districts were held by a patchwork of militias, with massacres such as the Afshar killings of 1993.

Tens of thousands of civilians died, perhaps 25,000 to 50,000 in Kabul alone, and a large part of it was left in ruins. Many Afghans, tired of warlords, were ready to welcome anyone who promised order.

The Taliban, who appeared around Kandahar in 1994, took Kabul in September 1996. Massoud withdrew to the north and fought on.
sum: The fighting among the victorious mujahideen after the fall of Kabul in April 1992, which wrecked much of the capital and prepared the way for the Taliban.
